processing: Usually made as sencha (often deep-steamed in Kagoshima), and widely used for gyokuro, kabusecha and tencha; a light final firing keeps its sweetness.
harvest_season: Early budding: first flush from early-to-mid April in Kagoshima, late April elsewhere; sensitive to late frost.
appearance_dry: Fine needles of a notably bright, vivid green, finer than Yabukita.
appearance_liquor: Vivid, clear light green with a sheen; deeper and greener than most sencha.
taste_profile: Sweet, smooth and rich in umami with very low astringency, a fresh, almost melon-like aroma and a clean finish; it tastes shaded even when it is not.

brewing.notes: Keep the water cool (65–70 °C) to make the most of the sweetness; it has little bitterness to worry about and gives a lovely cold brew.

vintage_note: Sold as a single-cultivar lot of the current year's first flush, often among the first shincha of the season from Kagoshima in April and from Yame slightly later; it also appears as the named cultivar in gyokuro and competition-grade teas. It carries a premium over Yabukita. Finish within the year, sealed and cold.
description:
Saemidori is the modern star among Japanese tea cultivars: a cross of Yabukita and Asatsuyu registered in 1990, which kept Yabukita's vigour and took Asatsuyu's sweetness and vivid colour. The name means something like 'clear green', and that is what you get, a bright, sweet, umami-rich tea with almost no astringency, which tastes shaded even when it was not.

It buds early, 4 to 7 days before Yabukita, which makes it a favourite for the first shincha of the year in Kagoshima and Yame and also leaves it vulnerable to late frost, one reason it is grown mainly in the warm south. It is made as sencha (often deep-steamed in Kagoshima), and it is also used for gyokuro, where its high amino-acid content is an asset.

Brew it cool, 65–70 °C, 5 g for 150 ml and a minute, and it gives a vivid, clear green cup that is sweet, smooth and thick with umami, with a fresh melon-like aroma and a clean finish; hotter water does not ruin it, it simply gives you a slightly brisker tea with less of the sweetness. Cold-brewed it is one of the best teas in Japan.

It is sold as a labelled single-cultivar sencha of the current year's first flush, and it carries a premium over Yabukita; it also appears by name in gyokuro and competition-grade teas from Yame and Kagoshima. Shincha lots arrive from mid-April in Kagoshima. Store it like sencha and finish it within the year.

Taste it next to its parent Asatsuyu and next to Yabukita, and you can see what the breeders were aiming for.
history:
Saemidori comes from a 1969 cross of Asatsuyu and Yabukita and registered only in 1990 as cultivar number 40. The name is given as clear green.

It was intended for sencha and has since moved into deep-steamed tea and gyokuro as well. It can be picked 4 to 7 days before Yabukita but suffers from frost and recovers poorly, so it is grown mainly in Kyushu, Kagoshima above all.
